identity.title: Right lower quadrant pain with periumbilical-to-RLQ migration

technique.how: Ask where the pain started and where it is now, and in what order symptoms appeared. Migration means a vague periumbilical or epigastric (visceral) pain that, over hours, shifts to a sharper localised RLQ (parietal) pain; also ask whether pain preceded vomiting and about anorexia.
technique.prerequisites: Patient able to give a history; for children or cognitively impaired patients, use carer history.

interpretation.positive_finding: Classic periumbilical-to-RLQ migration raises the probability of appendicitis (pediatric pooled LR+ 4.8 in undifferentiated abdominal pain; adult OR 2.2), more than RLQ pain alone.
interpretation.negative_finding: Lack of migration makes appendicitis less likely but many confirmed cases present with RLQ pain from the outset, so absence does not exclude it.
interpretation.pitfalls: Migration is reported in only about half of cases and is recalled unreliably; retrocaecal or pelvic appendices localise atypically. Vomiting before pain onset argues against appendicitis.
interpretation.changes_what: Migration present: treat as likely appendicitis, obtain imaging or surgical review; absent: keep appendicitis on the differential but weigh alternatives.

estimates.population: ED pediatric patients with undifferentiated abdominal pain; pooled from included studies (systematic review of 21 studies, 8605 patients overall)
estimates.reference_standard: Surgical pathology or clinical follow-up as defined per study
estimates.quote: history of "pain migration to right lower quadrant (RLQ)" (LR+ = 4.81, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 3.59-6.44)

estimates.target_condition: Acute appendicitis (migration of pain to right iliac fossa)
estimates.population: Adults and children admitted with acute abdominal pain up to 7 days, Mora Hospital Sweden (n=2478; 274 appendicitis)
estimates.reference_standard: Final diagnosis after appendectomy/histology and 1-year medical record review
estimates.quote: right-sided rectal tenderness (2.53), migration of pain to the right iliac fossa (2.18), and local guarding (2.11)

sources.citation: Wagner JM, McKinney WP, Carpenter JL. Does this patient have appendicitis? JAMA. 1996;276(19):1589-1594.

Benabbas R, Hanna M, Shah J, Sinert R. Diagnostic Accuracy of History, Physical Examination, Laboratory Tests, and Point-of-care Ultrasound for Pediatric Acute Appendicitis in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2017;24(5):523-551.
Laurell H, Hansson LE, Gunnarsson U. Manifestations of acute appendicitis: a prospective study on acute abdominal pain. Dig Surg. 2014;30(4-6):283-289.
Bundy DG, Byerley JS, Liles EA, Perrin EM, Katznelson J, Rice HE. Does this child have appendicitis? JAMA. 2007;298(4):438-451.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of migration to exclude appendicitis in young children, the elderly, pregnancy or patients with unreliable histories.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Migration followed by sudden generalised pain and rigidity suggests perforation: urgent surgical review.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Self-reported symptom sequence is subject to recall bias; the pediatric RCE notes only fair agreement for history items.

extraction_notes: Adult RCE (Wagner 1996) migration LR+ ~3.1-3.4 / LR- ~0.5 is not visible in the abstract or reachable full text, so not entered. Pediatric pooled LR+ 4.81 from Benabbas 2017 abstract (undifferentiated abdominal pain subgroup; the 'suspected AA' subgroup showed no strong association). Bundy 2007 abstract gives migration LR range 1.9-3.1 (children) without a point estimate, so it is cited but not entered. Laurell 2014 adult odds ratio 2.18 entered with LR null because OR is not an LR.
